summary: Most Indians (Hindus, Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists, Christians, Parsis) can leave their estate freely by will; Muslims can will at most one third. Dependants have maintenance claims against the estate. The Trusts Act 1882 allows private trusts, but India has no Hague Trusts Convention membership and no private foundation law.
family_claims: Hindu dependants can claim maintenance from the estate (Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act 1956, ss. 21-23). Muslims: bequests are capped at one third of the net estate under Muslim personal law, with fixed shares for heirs, so for Muslims heirship is forced.
foreign_law_note: Indian Succession Act 1925 s. 5: succession to immovable property in India follows Indian law wherever the deceased was domiciled; movables follow the law of the country of domicile at death. Part II does not apply to Hindus, Muslims, Buddhists, Sikhs and Jains. A foreigner domiciled abroad keeps foreign law for movables.
trust_note: Not on the HCCH status table. Private trusts are governed by the Indian Trusts Act 1882; public charitable trusts by state laws. Non-profit foundations are set up as Section 8 companies or charitable trusts; there is no private family foundation statute. Trust income is taxed under the Income-tax law's trust provisions (discretionary trusts at maximum rate). Foreign remittances follow FEMA rules.
open_questions: Confirm which sections of the Income-tax Act 2025 (from 1 April 2026) replace the old trust provisions.
Confirm the one-third limit for Muslims against the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937 and case law.
